articleTitle: Hug a hacker - or just have them killed? [editorial]
abstract: How, when caught, should hackers be punished? There is widespread debate in the specialist and mainstream media on this question. Suggestions range from the sublime to the spiteful. Controversial economist Steven Landsburg asks "If we execute murderers, why don't we execute the people who write computer worms? It would probably be a better investment." Landsburg compares the deterrential cost benefits of executing a murderer against those of dispatching what he coins a `vermiscripter' (author of a worm, virus, or Trojan).

BLADE SERVERS are cutting gaily into the server market, with their total share predicted by IDC to increase from 4.6% at $2.5bn in 2005, to 20% at $10bn in 2009. This growth is being driven by a demand for `high-density` computing, as blades are better equipped to meet this demand than rack-mounted or standalone servers.

You wouldn't expect a computer printer to be made from the same stuff that you thicken sauce with, but the computer industry will try anything once. Hewlett-Packard trialed a printer made of biodegradable cornstarch-based plastics in a bid to produce a 'greener' product. It was, in short, a printer that you could compost at the end of its life.

abstract: Alternatives to the 'one-CPU-in-steam' approach to enterprise computing are coming out of the defence, supercomputing and 'advancedscientific' R&D hothouses, and increasingly into the mainstream.

EMAIL TAKES HUGE VOLUMES of storage space, so email management systems capable of controlling copies and making intelligent decisions about what to keep or delete are a necessity. And, with email such an important part of business and records management, email management applications must also be capable of fast search and retrieval by a variety of different parameters and across multiple storage devices.

abstract: NETWORK ATTACHED STORAGE (NAS) is as old as the network itself, and, until recently, had changed little in the two decades since it was invented by Novell to overcome the limitations of disk drives attached directly to file servers.

THE SOARING POWER of server hardware, recently boosted by multicore processors, has focused IT managers' minds on how much power - both electrical and compute - they were wasting. Many servers installed with software like Active Directory may only see average utilisation of 20% or less. These are good candidates for virtualisation. Consolidating several of these types of underused server still leaves spare capacity to accommodate overhead demanded by the virtualisation software, which can account for 20% of overall processing time depending on the software used.

THE PRINCIPLES OF E-COMMERCE are robust enough to work - despite the lack of standardisation on the Internet. So within the controlled confines of an organisation they should flourish. E-commerce models vary according to the product or service being sold. Intranets have proved popular within organisations at providing standard information. As the functionality of websites increases, our demands on our organisations' Intranets will increase too.

articleTitle: How sam savvy is your enterprise?
abstract: An important milestone in software ownership was reached at the end of January 2006 - one that went unnoticed by the majority of enterprise users, yet one that will affect users everywhere. We're talking of the official release, by the International Standards Organisation (ISO), of the the Final Draft International Standard (FDIS) 19770-1 - a brand new ISO standard that deals with Software Asset Management.

articleTitle: Stating the case for chartered status for techies - [editorial]
abstract: Despite the obvious benefits, not everyone in the IT sector is convinced of the value of chartered status for its professionals. Indeed, over the last 20 years, the IT industry has in some respects been rather indifferent toward the notion. The reasons for this apparent coolness are many and varied. IT is still a relatively new profession, and has evolved at a breakneck pace compared with other disciplines. And, partly because of the unique mix of diversity and specificity in its make-up, consensus over issues of professionalism has proved hard to pin down.

articleTitle: IT depts must prove their value on their own terms - editorial
abstract: Toward the end of a recent report from the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) is a phrase that will give IT professionals pause for thought for the future: `The end of the IT department as we know it'. It's not the headline finding: the main nub of the EIU's `The Changing Role of IT in the Business' is the expectation gap that is broadening between senior executives and the IT function. Whereas many IT practitioners retain a `strong belief in the primacy of IT's cost-reduction role', says the report, within three years a coalition of IT managers and board level executives expect IT's primary role to shift to enabling revenue growth.

articleTitle: The network is the law (probably) - analysis
abstract: MOORE'S LAW has got a lot to answer for. What started out as an observation of a trend - albeit one that has held-up pretty well for 40 years - has encouraged people to come up with a bunch of other 'laws' that describe what technology can do. Few had the benefit of actual figures on which to base the trend that might become the law.

articleTitle: The IT professional: a social history - [summer special]

abstract: COLOSSUS WAS DEVELOPED to break German Geheimschreiber ciphers, and made a crucial contribution to the allied victory - and to the nascent UK computer industry. Its story is told for the first time in Colossus: Bletchley Park's Greatest Secret, published by Atlantic Books.

abstract: EVERY INFORMATION technologist has heard the call for `business service management': mapping the activities and spend in IT to the needs and priorities of the business at large. It's been an explicitly stated IT goal since the dawn of the discipline.

DIGITAL CRIMINALS do not need to steal your credit card details or go through your bins to obtain the data they need to defraud you: they can just go to your company system. People fear elite Russian hackers who bounce their attacks off many servers to hide their tracks, and make it virtually impossible to detect them until it is too late. But, in actual fact, the most prevalent threats come from within an organisation.

articleTitle: Health & safety: what every it professional should know
abstract: INFORMATION PROFESSIONALS are mostly employed in offices, but their working environment is often quite unlike that of colleagues in other departments. IT staff whose job role requires them to spend a lot of time in close proximity to densities of computer kit are likely to find themselves spending much of their working day in surroundings configured to meet the needs of machine, rather than man.

BETWEEN HALF and three-quarters of new products will fail each year. Most UK companies fear failure, but that failure can lead to unexpected success. For all companies, but particularly those in the IT sector, making the most of your intellectual property assets is a must. These are the company's crown jewels, but they should not be so tightly locked up that they cannot be used to their utmost. The solution to a struggling product already exists within most organisations - it just needs to be found; and, to find it, a culture of innovation must be inculcated.
